title: Select is switch/case for concurrency!
text:
Animals explain the select concurrency statement


An early try at programming-with-cartoons, in the spirit of _why’s Poignant Guide. Current work is at home.


read the transcript!


bubble 1: guy asks bird

What is select?

bubble 2: bird explains

It’s a control structure for concurrency. And Rob Pike, one of Golang’s developers, says it’s the reason channels and goroutines are built-in to the language.

bubble 3: guy asks “how does it work?”

Bird answers “It waits until 1 channel is ready. Kind of like case, and then runs the code in the corresponding branch.”

bubble 4: bird explains lines in Rob Pike’s example

{% highlight golang linenos %} select { case v1 := <-c1: fmt.Printf(“received %v from c1”, v1) case v2 := <-c2: // bird says here it is fanning in from c1 and c2 to stdout fmt.Printf(“received %v from c2”, v1) case c3 <- 23: fmt.Printf(“sent %v to c3”, 23) default: // giraffe says you can give a default if no channel is ready fmt.Printf(“no one was ready to communicate”) } {% endhighlight %}
Finally a cow explains if more than 1 channel is ready, then select picks on branch pseudorandomly.

title: Trigonometry 3: sin² + cos² = 1
text: Cover the right-hand column. Answer each question in your head, then look.

title: Trigonometry 3: sin² + cos² = 1
text:
First, why Pythagoras is true
The proof rests on Pythagoras, so recall why it holds. A right triangle has legs a and b and long side c.








On the left, four copies of the triangle sit in a square of side a + b. What is left over in the middle?
A tilted square, c by c: area c².


On the right, the same four triangles are moved into two pairs. What is left over now?
Two squares: a by a and b by b. Area a² + b².


The big square is the same, and so are the four triangles. So?
The leftovers have the same area: a² + b² = c².



Nothing was measured; the triangles only moved.

title: Trigonometry 3: sin² + cos² = 1
text:
The proof

It takes two steps.







Step 1. What are cos θ and sin θ?
By definition (part 1), the point at θ on the circle of radius 1 is (cos θ, sin θ).


Step 2. The triangle’s legs and long side?
cos θ across, sin θ up, and the radius, 1.


What does Pythagoras say?
cos²θ + sin²θ = 1.


What does sin²θ mean?
(sin θ)², the number sin θ squared. Not sin(θ²).


Does it only work in the first quadrant?
No. On the left cos θ is negative, but its square isn’t. Every point on the circle works.


At 0° or 90° there is no triangle.
The point is still 1 from the centre: (1, 0) or (0, 1). 1² + 0² = 1.



That is the whole proof: the definition, then Pythagoras.






NoteThe Pythagorean Identity



sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, for every angle θ. It is Pythagoras on the circle of radius 1.


Check it with part 1’s triangle at 30°: (1/2)² + (√3/2)² = 1/4 + 3/4 = 1.

title: Trigonometry 3: sin² + cos² = 1
text:
Using it








sin θ = 3/5, and θ is in quadrant II. What is cos²θ?
1 − (3/5)² = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25.


So cos θ?
√(16/25) = 4/5, or −4/5.


Which one?
Quadrant II is on the left, where across is negative: −4/5.


tan θ?
sin ÷ cos = (3/5) ÷ (−4/5) = −3/4.


Why did we need the quadrant?
The identity gives cos², and squaring hides the sign. The picture puts it back.



Someone writes: “sin θ = 0.6, so cos θ = 0.4, because they add to 1.” Find the mistake.
Decide before you read on.
The squares add to 1, not the numbers. 0.6² = 0.36, so cos²θ = 0.64, and cos θ = 0.8 (in quadrant I).

title: Trigonometry 3: sin² + cos² = 1
text:
Simplifying
The identity is a swap: 1 can become sin² + cos², and back.







Simplify 1 − cos²θ.
sin²θ.


Simplify (1 − sin²θ) ÷ cos θ.
cos²θ ÷ cos θ = cos θ.


Divide sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 by cos²θ. What do you get?
tan²θ + 1 = sec²θ: a second identity, free.

title: Trigonometry 3: sin² + cos² = 1
text:
Exercises
Click Answer under an exercise to see it.

cos θ = 5/13, and θ is in quadrant IV. Find sin θ and tan θ.


Answer

sin²θ = 1 − 25/169 = 144/169. Quadrant IV is below, so sin θ = −12/13, and tan θ = (−12/13) ÷ (5/13) = −12/5.

cos θ = −0.6, and θ is in quadrant III. Find sin θ and tan θ.


Answer

sin²θ = 1 − 0.36 = 0.64. Quadrant III is below, so sin θ = −0.8, and tan θ = −0.8 ÷ −0.6 = 4/3.

Simplify:

sin²θ + cos²θ + tan²θ
cos θ · tan θ
1 ÷ cos²θ − 1



Answer


1 + tan²θ = sec²θ.
cos θ · (sin θ ÷ cos θ) = sin θ.
sec²θ − 1 = tan²θ.


Check the identity at 45° with part 1’s other triangle.


Answer

(√2/2)² + (√2/2)² = 2/4 + 2/4 = 1.

title: Trigonometry 3: sin² + cos² = 1
text:
The unit on one page

An angle is a walk round the circle of radius 1; π radians = 180°.
The walk ends at (cos θ, sin θ); tan = sin ÷ cos, and sec, csc, cot are one over cos, sin, tan.
The reference angle gives the numbers; the quadrant gives the sign.
The graphs are heights and distances across, drawn against the walk; y = A sin(B(x − h)) + k has amplitude |A|, period 2π/B, midline k.
A graph breaks where the thing it divides by is 0.
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1: Pythagoras on the circle.

title: Trigonometry 1: a point on a circle
text:
An angle is a walk







A circle has radius 1. Walk once round it. How far did you go?
2π, its circumference.


Half way round?
π.


How many degrees is half a turn?
180°.


So what is an angle?
How far you walked round the circle. Degrees count 360 to a turn; radians count the distance itself, 2π to a turn.


A quarter turn, in radians?
2π ÷ 4 = π/2.


π/3, in degrees?
π is 180°, so π/3 is 60°.


135°, in radians?
135 is three quarters of 180, so 3π/4.









NoteThe Law of Radians



π radians = 180°. To get radians, multiply degrees by π/180; to get degrees, multiply radians by 180/π.
crumbs: Trigonometry 1: a point on a circle

title: Trigonometry 1: a point on a circle
text:
Where the walk ends
Start at (1, 0) and walk θ round the circle, anticlockwise.








Where are you now?
At some point (x, y) on the circle.


What is x called?
cos θ: how far across.


And y?
sin θ: how far up.


What is tan θ?
sin θ ÷ cos θ: up over across, the slope of your radius.









NoteThe Law of the Point



The point at angle θ on the circle of radius 1 is (cos θ, sin θ).


A bigger circle is the same picture, scaled. That is all a right triangle is.







A 4 m ladder leans at 60° to the ground. Which circle is it the radius of?
The circle of radius 4.


How high does it reach?
4 times as high as on the unit circle: 4 sin 60°.


A ramp 2 m long rises 1 m. Which angle has sin θ = 1/2?
We need a few values we know by heart. Next section.
crumbs: Trigonometry 1: a point on a circle

title: Trigonometry 1: a point on a circle
text:
Two triangles worth knowing








Cut a square along its diagonal. The angles?
45°, 45°, 90°.


Make the diagonal 1. How long are the two equal sides, x?
x² + x² = 1, so x = 1/√2 = √2/2.


So cos 45° and sin 45°?
Both √2/2.


Cut an equilateral triangle with sides 1 in half. The angles?
30°, 60°, 90°.


The short side?
Half of 1: 1/2. That’s sin 30°.


The long side?
√(1 − 1/4) = √3/2. That’s cos 30°.


Back to the ramp: the angle?
sin θ = 1/2, so θ = 30°.


And the ladder: 4 sin 60°?
Turn the 30-60-90 triangle round: sin 60° = √3/2. The ladder reaches 4 · √3/2 = 2√3 ≈ 3.46 m.
crumbs: Trigonometry 1: a point on a circle

title: Trigonometry 1: a point on a circle
text:
Same reference angle, same numbers








Where is 150°?
30° short of half a turn: 30° mirrored across the up-down axis.


So sin 150°?
The same height as 30°: 1/2.


And cos 150°?
The same distance across, but to the left: −√3/2.


What is 30° called here?
The reference angle: the angle between your radius and the nearest x-axis.


The reference angle of 225°?
225 − 180 = 45°.


Of 300°?
360 − 300 = 60°.









NoteThe Law of Reference Angles



An angle has the same sin and cos as its reference angle, except for the sign. The quadrant sets the sign: across is negative on the left, up is negative below.


Someone writes sin 210° = 1/2. Find the mistake.
Decide before you read on.
210° is 30° past half a turn, below the axis. Below means up is negative: sin 210° = −1/2.

title: Trigonometry 1: a point on a circle
text:
The other three







sec θ?
1 ÷ cos θ.


csc θ?
1 ÷ sin θ.


cot θ?
1 ÷ tan θ, which is cos θ ÷ sin θ.


sec 60°?
cos 60° = 1/2, so sec 60° = 2.


tan 90°?
At 90° you are at (0, 1). cos 90° = 0, and we can’t divide by 0. No value.



The names cross over: sec goes with cos, csc with sin. If that won’t stick, remember only “one over”.

Exercises
Click Answer under an exercise to see it.

Turn 270° into radians, and 2π/3 into degrees.


Answer

3π/2; 120°.

Turn 135° into radians, and 5π/6 into degrees.


Answer

Draw the point first, then give sin 210° and cos 120°.


Answer

210° is below the axis on the left: sin 210° = −1/2. 120° is up and to the left: cos 120° = −1/2.

csc(π/4) and cot 150°.


Answer

π/4 is 45°, sin 45° = √2/2, so csc(π/4) = 2/√2 = √2. cot 150° = cos 150° ÷ sin 150° = (−√3/2) ÷ (1/2) = −√3.

The reference angles of 225° and 300°.


Answer

45° and 60°.

A 10 m ramp rises at 30°. How high does it go?


Answer

10 sin 30° = 10 · 1/2 = 5 m.

A 2 m pole leans against a wall; its top is √2 m up. At what angle does it lean?


Answer

sin θ = √2/2, so θ = 45°.

title: Linear algebra 4: two orthogonal bases
text:
Cover the right-hand column. Answer each question in your head, then look.
Part 3 ended with a promise: an orthogonal basis for every matrix. Here is one that isn’t symmetric:
\[
A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}
\]

title: Linear algebra 4: two orthogonal bases
text:
Its eigenvectors aren’t enough







Is A symmetric?
No. Its first row is (3, 0); its first column is (3, 4).


What is A(0, 1)?
(0, 5). Stretched by 5, not turned.


What is A(1, −2)?
(3, −6). Stretched by 3, not turned.


So (0, 1) and (1, −2) are eigenvectors of A. Are they orthogonal?
(0, 1)·(1, −2) = −2. No.


Then can we find coordinates by projection?
No. Part 3’s opening picture showed why.


And the shear S = (1 1; 0 1) from part 2?
Worse: only one line of eigenvectors.



So we ask for less. We don’t need an arrow to keep its line. We need two orthogonal arrows going in that come out still orthogonal.

title: Linear algebra 4: two orthogonal bases
Linear algebra 4: two orthogonal bases
text:
The three steps, once more
Take x = (2, 0) again. In comes v₁ = (1, 1) and v₂ = (−1, 1); out go u₁ along (3, 9) and u₂ along (−3, 1).







Step 1: x’s coordinates in v’s?
By projection, since the v’s are orthogonal: 2/2 = 1 of v₁, −2/2 = −1 of v₂.


Step 2: what does A do to each basis vector?
Sends v₁ to (3, 9), and v₂ to (−3, 1).


Step 3: so where does x go?
1·(3, 9) − 1·(−3, 1) = (6, 8).


Check the long way: A(2, 0)?
(3·2 + 0·0, 4·2 + 5·0) = (6, 8). The same.


In part 3, the same P turned back and turned again. Here?
Two different turns: V for the arrow going in, U for the arrow coming out.



Make every basis vector length 1 (orthonormal), as in part 3, and the steps become three matrices:
\[
V = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} {\color{#7570B3}1} & {\color{#D95F02}-1} \\ {\color{#7570B3}1} & {\color{#D95F02}1} \end{pmatrix}\qquad
\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{45} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt5 \end{pmatrix}\qquad
U = \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{pmatrix} {\color{#7570B3}1} & {\color{#D95F02}-3} \\ {\color{#7570B3}3} & {\color{#D95F02}1} \end{pmatrix}
\]
\[
A = U\,\Sigma\,V^{\mathsf T}
\]







Read right to left: what does Vᵀ do?
Projects x onto the v’s: x’s coordinates in v’s.


And Σ?
Stretches each coordinate, by σ₁ and σ₂.


And U?
Builds the result from the u’s.


What does Lay call the v’s and the u’s?
The right and left singular vectors (7.4).


Why insist that both bases are orthonormal?
So every coordinate, going in and coming out, is a measurement (part 3): lengths survive, and keeping the biggest σ’s gives the nearest approximation.


How is this different from part 2’s P D P⁻¹?
Two bases instead of one.


Does every matrix have one?
Yes, every one. Even the shear S: its v₁ leans at about 58°, and its σ’s are 1.618 and 0.618.









NoteThe Law of Two Bases



Every matrix sends some orthogonal arrows to orthogonal arrows. A = U Σ Vᵀ: project onto the v’s, stretch, build with the u’s. This is the singular value decomposition, SVD.

title: Linear algebra 4: two orthogonal bases
text:
Where the v’s come from
We found 45° by turning v₁ until it worked. There is a shortcut, and it uses part 3.
\[
A^{\mathsf T} A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 25 & 20 \\ 20 & 25 \end{pmatrix}
\]







Is AᵀA symmetric?
Yes. Row 1 is (25, 20); so is column 1.


So what do we know about its eigenvectors?
Part 3: they are orthogonal.


What are they?
(1, 1), eigenvalue 45, and (−1, 1), eigenvalue 5. Our v’s.


And 45 and 5?
σ₁² and σ₂².

title: Linear algebra 4: two orthogonal bases
text:
What survives, and what’s lost







In A = UΣVᵀ, which part changes area?
Only Σ. The turns keep area.


So what is det A, up to sign?
σ₁σ₂ = √45·√5 = 15. Check: 3·5 − 0·4 = 15.


What if a σ is 0?
That direction is flattened to 0.











Take F = (1 1; 1 1). What is F(1, −1)?
(0, 0).


What are F’s σ’s?
2 and 0. The circle goes flat, onto a segment.


Can any matrix undo F?
No. F sends (1, −1) and (0, 0) to the same place; nothing can tell them apart again.


What does Lay call the number of nonzero σ’s?
The rank (7.4). F has rank 1.


And the flattened directions?
The null space (4.2).

title: Linear algebra 4: two orthogonal bases
section: Why anyone bothers: the best line
text:
Why anyone bothers: the best line
Part 3 ended with the nearest point: in an orthonormal basis, keeping one coordinate gives the projection, as close as that direction can get. Now we choose the direction.
Read A’s rows as two points, (3, 0) and (4, 5).








For a length-1 arrow v, what are the two numbers in Av?
Row 1 dotted with v, and row 2 dotted with v: each point’s projection onto v’s line, as a signed length.


Which v makes Av longest?
v₁. A stretches it most: the long axis of the ellipse.


So which line gets the longest projections?
The one along v₁ = (1, 1).


Why is that the line closest to the points?
Each point’s length is fixed. Projection² + distance² = length², so the longer the projection, the shorter the distance.


And with a thousand rows?
The same: v₁ is the line through the origin that passes closest to all of them.









NoteThe Law of the Best Line



A’s first in-arrow v₁ is the line that passes closest to A’s rows.


Make each row a photo of a face, and v₁, v₂, … become the “eigenfaces” that most faces are mostly made of. That story is told in the SVD comic, which follows Hopcroft and Kannan from best fit to principal components.

title: Linear algebra 2: the basis where it only stretches
text:
Cover the right-hand column. Answer each question in your head, then look.
Part 1 ended with a matrix that turns most arrows but leaves two directions alone:
\[
A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
\]
This part uses those two directions as the basis.

title: Linear algebra 2: the basis where it only stretches
crumbs: Linear algebra 2: the basis where it only stretches

title: Linear algebra 2: the basis where it only stretches
section: What does A do to x?
text:
What does A do to x?
Call the two eigenvectors v₁ = (1, 1) and v₂ = (−1, 1), and take one arrow to work with, x = (2, 0): its coordinates in the standard basis.
Where does A send x? We could multiply A by x. Instead we’ll take three easy steps.
Step 1. Translate x into v’s.







What are x’s coordinates in v’s?
(1, −1), because 1·v₁ − 1·v₂ = (1, 1) − (−1, 1) = (2, 0).



Step 2. Stretch.







What does A do to v₁?
Stretches it by 3.


And to v₂?
Leaves it as it is: a stretch by 1.


So what are Ax’s coordinates in v’s?
(3·1, 1·(−1)) = (3, −1).



Step 3. Translate back into the usual grid.







What is (3, −1) in v’s, in the usual grid?
3·v₁ − 1·v₂ = (3, 3) − (−1, 1) = (4, 2).


Check the long way: what is A(2, 0)?
(2·2 + 1·0, 1·2 + 2·0) = (4, 2). The same.
crumbs: Linear algebra 2: the basis where it only stretches

title: Linear algebra 2: the basis where it only stretches
text:
Naming the steps
We did the three steps with numbers. Each one is also a matrix. Name them, and A fits on one line.







Step 3 translates from v’s into the usual grid. Have we met that?
Yes: part 1’s change-of-coordinates matrix, P. Its columns are v₁ and v₂.


Step 1 goes the other way. What is it?
P undone. Call it P⁻¹.



\[
P^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac12 & \tfrac12 \\ -\tfrac12 & \tfrac12 \end{pmatrix}\qquad
P^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac12\cdot 2 + \tfrac12\cdot 0 \\ -\tfrac12\cdot 2 + \tfrac12\cdot 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}
\]







Does it undo P?
Yes. P⁻¹ takes (2, 0) to (1, −1), and P takes (1, −1) back to (2, 0).


Why the −1?
As 3⁻¹ = ⅓ undoes multiplying by 3. Say “P inverse”.


Step 2 only stretches. What is it?
D, a matrix with the eigenvalues on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere: a diagonal matrix.



\[
P = \begin{pmatrix} {\color{#7570B3}1} & {\color{#D95F02}-1} \\ {\color{#7570B3}1} & {\color{#D95F02}1} \end{pmatrix}\qquad
D = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\qquad
A = P\,D\,P^{-1}
\]







Why is P⁻¹ on the right, when it’s step 1?
A matrix acts on what’s to its right, so P D P⁻¹ x is read right to left: P⁻¹ first, P last.



Writing A = P D P⁻¹ is called diagonalizing A (Lay 5.3).






NoteThe Law of Stretching



Use a matrix’s eigenvectors as the basis, and the matrix only stretches. A = P D P⁻¹: find the coordinates, stretch them, change back.
crumbs: Linear algebra 2: the basis where it only stretches

title: Linear algebra 2: the basis where it only stretches
text:
Why anyone bothers







What is A applied ten times to x?
Ten matrix multiplications, if done the long way.


And in v’s?
Stretch the coordinates ten times: (3¹⁰·1, 1¹⁰·(−1)) = (59049, −1).


So what is A¹⁰x?
59049·(1, 1) − 1·(−1, 1) = (59050, 59048).


How much work was that?
One look-up, one power of each number, one translation back.



Lay’s 5.3, Example 2 does the same with another matrix:
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 7 & 2 \\ -4 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = P\,D\,P^{-1}\qquad
P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}\qquad
D = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}
\]







What is its k-th power?
P Dᵏ P⁻¹. Only the 5ᵏ and the 3ᵏ change.
crumbs: Linear algebra 2: the basis where it only stretches

title: Linear algebra 2: the basis where it only stretches
text:
Same map, new matrix
Part 1 changed the basis and kept the arrow. Now we change the basis and keep the map.







In the usual grid, A’s matrix is (2 1; 1 2). In v’s, what is it?
D = (3 0; 0 1). In v’s, A only stretches.


Are A and D two different maps?
No. One map, written in two bases. Lay calls such matrices similar.


What changed between them?
The entries.


What didn’t?
What belongs to the map itself: the eigenvalues, 3 and 1, for a start.



One more number belongs to the map: how much it scales area.








What does A do to the unit square?
Makes the parallelogram on (2, 1) and (1, 2), of area 2·2 − 1·1 = 3.


And D?
Makes a 3 × 1 rectangle: area 3. The same, because it’s the same map.


What is that number called?
The determinant. For (a b; c d), det = ad − bc.



To check your understanding: a friend says A’s eigenvalues are its diagonal entries, 2 and 2. Are they right? Decide before you read on.







Is 2 an eigenvalue of A?
No. A’s eigenvalues are 3 and 1.


When are the diagonal entries the eigenvalues?
When the matrix is diagonal, like D. Entries depend on the basis; eigenvalues don’t.









NoteThe Law of Invariance



A change of basis changes a matrix’s entries, not the map. What belongs to the map survives it: its eigenvalues, and its determinant.
crumbs: Linear algebra 2: the basis where it only stretches

title: Linear algebra 2: the basis where it only stretches
text:
Finding the eigenvalues yourself
So far, 3 and 1 were handed to you. Here is where they come from. I is the identity, (1 0; 0 1), the matrix that changes nothing.







If v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ, what does A − λI do to v?
Av − λv = λv − λv = 0. It flattens v to 0.


A matrix that flattens an arrow to 0 squashes the square onto a line. What area is left?
0. So det(A − λI) = 0.


For our A, what is A − λI?
(2−λ 1; 1 2−λ), so det(A − λI) = (2 − λ)² − 1.


When is (2 − λ)² − 1 = 0?
When 2 − λ = 1 or −1: λ = 1 or λ = 3.


Check λ = 3.
A − 3I = (−1 1; 1 −1) sends (1, 1) to (0, 0): the eigenvector, flattened.



det(A − λI) = 0 is Lay’s characteristic equation (5.2).
crumbs: Linear algebra 2: the basis where it only stretches

title: Linear algebra 2: the basis where it only stretches
section: Not every matrix is so kind
text:
Not every matrix is so kind
\[
S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\]







What is S(1, 0)?
(1, 0). Not turned.


What is S(0, 1)?
(1, 1). Turned.


Which arrows does S not turn?
Only those along (1, 0). One line.


How many basis vectors does a flat page need?
Two.


So can we write S = P D P⁻¹?
No. There aren’t enough eigenvectors.


Look back at A’s v₁ = (1, 1) and v₂ = (−1, 1). Notice anything?
They are perpendicular.


Is that luck?
No. A is symmetric: it is its own mirror across the diagonal. That is part 3.


And what about S?
Use two different bases, one for the arrow going in and one for the arrow coming out. That is SVD, part 4.

title: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing
text:
My drawing, made to talk with Runway Act-Two. Later in the course: how.
Lesson 1 gave you def and return with one input (parity). Lesson 2 gave you while, input() and f-strings. This lesson uses all of them. What is new: a function’s name, several inputs, how to pass those inputs (by position or by name), the difference between return and print, one function that calls another, and a function that wraps a call to Claude.
crumbs: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing

title: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing
section: A function is a name for a computation
text:
A function is a name for a computation
A function is a name for a computation: a recipe, a process, a rule you want to use again without writing it out again. Naming it well is the most important habit in this lesson. A good name says what the step is for, so the reader does not have to work out how it was made.
Lesson 1’s recipe took one input, n, and gave back a word. A recipe usually needs more than one input: the amount, the servings it was written for, and the servings you want. The three names in the parentheses after def are parameters: the boxes the function fills when you call it.
Type this into ~/course/scale.py. You will keep using this file:
def scaled(amount, base_servings, servings):
    return amount * servings / base_servings

print(f"Flour: {250 * 6 / 2} g")
print(f"Flour: {scaled(250, 2, 6)} g")
Both lines print 750.0 g. The first only says how the number was made; the second says what it means.
To check your understanding, ask Claude in the right pane: “Suggest three names for a function that turns a recipe’s base amount into the amount for any number of servings. Which name is best, and why?” Guess its top pick first.
crumbs: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing

title: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing
section: Names or positions for the inputs
text:
Names or positions for the inputs
A call can pass its inputs in two ways:

by position: scaled(250, 2, 6). Each value goes to the next parameter, in order.
by name: scaled(amount=250, base_servings=2, servings=6). Each value goes to the parameter with that name, in any order.

Use names when a wrong order would still run and still give an answer. Here the program does not stop when you swap two numbers. It prints 83.33333333333333 instead of 750.0, and nothing tells you it is wrong. The names make that mistake hard to make.
Use positions when the order is obvious and the call is short. parity(7) from lesson 1 has one input, so there is no order to get wrong.
Rule of thumb: if the reader would need to look up the function to know which value is which, name the inputs.
Which would you use, names or positions, for scaled with its three numbers, and for parity with its one? Then check your answers against the rule above.
crumbs: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing

title: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing
section: Reuse with input in the middle
text:
Reuse with input in the middle
One function can serve many ingredients, and the number can come from the user while the program is running. Add these lines to scale.py, below scaled:
servings = int(input("How many servings? "))
print(f"Flour: {scaled(amount=250, base_servings=2, servings=servings)} g")
print(f"Sugar: {scaled(amount=100, base_servings=2, servings=servings)} g")
Guess the two lines for 6, then run it and check. Then type 1. You wrote the rule once, in scaled, and it worked for two ingredients, with a number the program didn’t know until you typed it.
crumbs: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing

title: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing
section: Bug hunt: a recipe that prints instead
text:
Bug hunt: a recipe that prints instead
Claude wrote this version. It has one bug. Type it in scale_bug.py, run it, and find the bug. Claude will not say where it is.
def scaled(amount, base_servings, servings):
    print(amount * servings / base_servings)

total = scaled(amount=250, base_servings=2, servings=4) + 100
print(f"total: {total}")
For the bug:

Write down the error message.
Guess what is wrong, in one sentence.
Fix it, run it, and check the output by hand.

Then tell Claude, in the right pane, what you found, and ask only why the error happens.
crumbs: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing

title: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing
section: AI thread: wrap the call in a function
text:
AI thread: wrap the call in a function
Each time your program talks to Claude, the same lines repeat. Put them in one function, so the rest of the program only asks a question and gets a reply. Add this to frame.py, above the prints. Guess what the last line prints, then run it.
import subprocess

def ask(question):
    reply = subprocess.run(
        ["claude", "-p", question, "--tools", "",
         "--no-session-persistence"],
        capture_output=True, text=True)
    return reply.stdout.strip()

print(ask("Reply with only the word hello."))
ask is the one place the program talks to Claude. If the call needs to change, for example a new flag, you change it here and nowhere else. ask returns the reply and does not print it: the caller decides what to do with it.
crumbs: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing

title: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing
text:
A function that calls ask
Lesson 2’s shape program asked Claude for a turn angle, then turned that text into a number. Put that step in a function, and it can be reused by any program that needs an angle:
def angle_for(shape):
    reply = ask(f"How many degrees does a turtle turn at each corner of a {shape}? Reply with only the number.")
    return float(reply)

print(f"Pentagon turn: {angle_for('pentagon')} degrees")
sides = round(360 / angle_for("pentagon"))
print(f"Sides: {sides}")
Guess what the first line prints, and what sides comes to. The first call to angle_for has the whole chain behind it: angle_for calls ask, and ask calls Claude.
To check your understanding, ask Claude in the right pane: “Why does angle_for call ask instead of calling subprocess itself?” Guess the gist of its answer first.
If Claude’s reply is a sentence, float fails inside angle_for, and the error points at float, not at the question. A function that hides a step also hides where it went wrong, so read the traceback to the bottom to see which function failed.
crumbs: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing

title: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing
text:
Write your own program
Write a program of your own with at least two functions, one of which calls the other. Claude writes none of it.
Pick a theme from cooking, art, music, or fashion, and build something that takes at least two inputs, returns a value, and prints a line at the end in your theme’s words. One of your functions must ask Claude for a reply and return it, using ask from the AI thread above.
Simple ideas to start from, pick one:

a function that prices a frame from its width and height, and a second one that adds tax;
a function that scales a dough or a paint mix for any number of batches;
a function that asks Claude for a short name for any number you give it, and returns the name.

Before you run it, guess the output for two different sets of inputs. Name the inputs in any call where a wrong order would still run.
When it works, walk Claude through it, line by line. Claude will ask why each function takes the inputs it takes, and where it could fail, for example with a zero or a negative number. Claude will not fix anything.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Why are we doing this?
An AI can install software, add up numbers and write proofs faster than either of us ever will. So why learn any of it?
For the same reason people learned pure math long before anyone needed it. Almost nobody uses calculus at work. What it built was the ability to understand: to follow an argument, see why it holds, and notice when it doesn’t.
That’s the point of this course: not to get the computer to do things, but to understand what it did, and why, well enough to catch it when it’s wrong.
To check your understanding as you go, guess what each command will do before you run it. When the computer surprises you, that’s the interesting part: guess why, in your own words, check with Claude, and ask your teacher for help.






TipHow to use this page



This lesson is twelve short sessions, each one sitting of 15 to 30 minutes: setting up (the first three), Python (the next four), adding up 1 to 100 (three more) and Lean (the last two). Do one session, stop whenever you like, and come back: the list of sessions at the top of the page shows where you are and takes you back there.
Each grey box has a copy button in its top right corner. Paste into the terminal with Ctrl+Shift+V and press Enter. Read the sentence above each box before you run it.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Turn on Linux (WSL)
Underneath the windows and buttons, a computer works with text. A terminal is a window where you talk to it in words. We’ll use Linux, running inside Windows (that’s WSL, Windows Subsystem for Linux).

Click Start and type PowerShell.
Right-click Windows PowerShell, choose Run as administrator, and click Yes.
Paste this and press Enter:

wsl --install
When it says so, restart the computer. A window called Ubuntu (our kind of Linux) then opens and asks you to make up a username (short, lowercase, no spaces) and a password.






WarningThe password is invisible



When you type it, nothing appears, not even dots. That’s normal. Type it anyway and press Enter.


From now on, open Terminal from the Start menu and pick Ubuntu from the ▾ menu next to the tabs.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Look around
The line ending in $ is the prompt: the computer waiting for you.
pwd
pwd prints where you are, something like /home/anna: your home folder, written as a path (folders inside folders, separated by /).
mkdir course
cd course

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Stop the password questions
Commands starting with sudo run as the administrator, and Linux asks for your password each time. The Windows login already protects this computer, so we tell Linux to stop asking:
echo "$USER ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL" | sudo tee /etc/sudoers.d/$USER
sudo chmod 0440 /etc/sudoers.d/$USER

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Your tutor: Claude Code
Claude is an AI, a language model: it learned from a huge amount of text to predict what words come next. That turns out to be enough to explain things and write code. It also makes Claude very good at sounding right. Usually it is right. Sometimes it isn’t, and it can’t always tell. That’s why you check.
Claude Code lets you talk to Claude in the terminal. You’ll need a Claude account.
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
curl downloads the installer, and | bash runs it (the |, a pipe, sends one command’s output into the next).
Claude could do this whole lesson by itself. That’s why we tell it not to. This box writes a file called CLAUDE.md: standing instructions Claude reads every time it starts in this folder.
cat > ~/course/CLAUDE.md <<'EOF'
# Tutor mode

I'm a beginner learning to program, and above all to reason.
The point is that I work things out myself.
You're my tutor, not the one doing the work.

- Never write the code for my exercises,
  and don't run commands or edit files for me.
  If you solve it, the lesson is lost.
- If I paste an error message, explain in plain words
  what it means and where to look. One hint, not the fix.
- If I ask what a command does, explain it simply,
  then ask me to predict what will happen before I run it.
- Ask me "why?" often, and look for the hole
  in my explanations.
- If I ask how you work, or why AI gets things wrong,
  explain honestly and simply. That's part of the course.
- Allowed: if I ask for code *to referee*
  (with a hidden bug for me to find), write it.
- Keep answers short. Use everyday words.
EOF
Press Alt+Shift+D to split the window into two panes. In the right pane, start Claude:
cd ~/course
claude
The first time, it opens a browser to log in. Claude asks before it does anything on your computer: say no unless you understand what it’s asking.
Try two questions: “What did the cat > CLAUDE.md command I just ran do?” and “When are you most likely to be wrong?”
From now on: left pane, you work. Right pane, you ask.






TipAsking well



Claude only knows what you tell it. A good question says what you did, what happened, and what you think: “I ran python3 gauss.py and got this error: (paste). I think line 3 is wrong. Am I right?” Errors are normal. Read each one yourself first and guess, then paste it with your guess. Fixing it is your job.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
A friendlier shell: fish
The program that reads what you type is the shell. Ubuntu’s is bash. We’ll use fish, which helps you type less. Ask Claude what chsh does, and predict what will change, and when:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y fish
sudo chsh -s /usr/bin/fish $USER
(apt installs software.) Close the left pane (exit) and open a new one with Alt+Shift+D. Was your prediction right?
Fish suggests the rest of a command in grey from what you typed before (→ accepts it), and Tab finishes names. ↑ brings back earlier commands.
Fish doesn’t know yet where Claude was installed. Tell it once:
fish_add_path ~/.local/bin
To check your understanding (ask Claude if you’re stuck): what is a “path”, and why did bash find Claude but fish didn’t?

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
An editor: nvim
To write programs we need a text editor. nvim runs inside the terminal.
sudo apt install -y neovim
cd ~/course
nvim hello.txt
nvim has two modes, and most nvim confusion is forgetting which one you’re in:

Normal mode, where it starts: every key is a command. x deletes a letter, u undoes. Type a word here and each letter does something, usually something strange.
Insert mode: keys type letters, like any other editor. The bottom line says -- INSERT --.

i goes from normal to insert; Esc goes back. Why two modes? So every key can be a command without holding Ctrl. When in doubt, press Esc: it always lands you in normal mode, and a second press does no harm.



Press (in normal mode)
What it does




i
start typing (insert mode)


Esc
stop typing (from insert mode)


:wq Enter
save and quit


:q! Enter
quit without saving



Press i, type hello, press Esc, type :wq, press Enter. What will this print?
cat hello.txt
Everyone mistypes. In nvim, you fix things from normal mode:



Press (in normal mode)
What it does




arrow keys
move around


x
delete the letter under the cursor


u
undo (press again to undo more)


:5 Enter
jump to line 5



To add letters, move to the spot and press i; Backspace works while you’re in insert mode.
Try it: nvim hello.txt, press x. Which letter goes? Then u to bring it back. Still in normal mode, type ox. Does x delete a letter again? Decide before you read on.
o is a command too: open a new line below and switch to insert mode. So the x after it is just a letter, on a new line. Esc, then u until it’s hello again, and :wq.
Stuck in nvim? Press Esc a few times, then :q!. (More nvim: type :Tutor inside it.)

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words

Python
python3

2 + 2

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Boxes and questions
Start Python again and predict each line before pressing Enter:
python3
x = 5
x + 1
x
x = x + 1
x
x == 6
x == 7
x = 5 makes a box called x and puts 5 in it. x + 1 works out an answer but leaves the box alone.
In maths, x = x + 1 is nonsense. In Python, = means “work out the right side, then put it in the box on the left”.
== asks whether two things are equal, and the answer is True or False. One = stores, two == ask. Mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes in programming.
Leave Python with Ctrl+D.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Decisions: if
cd ~/course
nvim decide.py
Type this in (i first, Esc and :wq at the end):
n = 7
if n % 2 == 0:
    print(n, "is even")
else:
    print(n, "is odd")
% is the remainder: 7 % 2 is 1. if runs the indented lines under it when its question is True, otherwise the lines under else:. What will it print? Run it:
python3 decide.py

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Typos Python can’t see
Make a typo on purpose: in decide.py, change print on line 3 to pirnt, save and run it. Will Python complain? Decide before you read on.
It doesn’t. n is 7, so line 3 never runs, and Python only notices a mistake when it gets there. Now make the same typo on line 5 and run it again: NameError: name 'pirnt' is not defined, with the line number. Fix both with the keys from A shell and an editor: :3, :5, x and i. A program that ran once can still hide a mistake on a line it didn’t reach.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Indentation: what’s inside what
A line ending in : starts a block: the lines under it, indented 4 spaces further. The block ends at the first line that steps back out. nvim indents for you after a :, but it can’t know when a block ends. That’s you, pressing Backspace, and it’s a reasoning question: does this line belong inside?

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
The story
Around 1785, the story goes, a teacher told his class to add up every number from 1 to 100. A ten-year-old, Carl Friedrich Gauss, wrote the answer almost at once: 5050.
How might he have done it? Spend two minutes with a pencil before reading on.
crumbs: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
The slow way: a loop
A new program, so a new file (type it in yourself: typing teaches more than pasting):
cd ~/course
nvim gauss.py
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        total = total + k
        print(k, total)
    return total

print(sum_to(100))
sum_to(n) adds up 1 to n: total starts at 0 and the loop adds each k in turn. Work out the first three lines, then run it:
python3 gauss.py
The last two lines say 100 5050, the loop’s last step, and 5050, the answer return handed back to print.
Now make an error on purpose: delete the spaces in front of total = total + k and run it. Read the error, guess what it means, then paste it to Claude with your guess.






ImportantWhy n + 1?



Change range(1, n + 1) to range(1, n). What will the last line be? Run it. An AI makes exactly this kind of mistake, and you just learned to catch it.
crumbs: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Gauss’s trick
Write the sum forwards and backwards:
  1 +  2 +  3 + ... +  99 + 100
100 + 99 + 98 + ... +   2 +   1
Each column adds up to 101, and there are 100 columns. Two copies of the sum make 100 × 101 = 10100, so one copy is 5050. For any \(n\):
\[1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}\]
To check your understanding, explain it to Claude in your own words, without the picture, and let it look for the hole. (Does your explanation work when \(n\) is odd?)
crumbs: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
A check inside the loop
assert means “this must be true here”. Try it in python3, predicting each line first:
python3
assert 4 % 2 == 0
assert 4 % 2 == 1
The first is true, so nothing happens. The second is false, and Python stops with an AssertionError. (Ctrl+D to leave.)
Now put one inside the loop, in a copy of gauss.py:
cp gauss.py invariant.py
nvim invariant.py
Replace print(k, total) with the assert (:5 Enter jumps to it, then cc):
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        total = total + k
        assert 2 * total == k * (k + 1)
    return total

print(sum_to(100))
So this loop checks Gauss’s formula after every step. What should it print? Run it:
python3 invariant.py
It prints 5050: no step failed.
Now break the loop on purpose: change total + k to total + k + 1. At which k will the assert stop it? Then change it back.
crumbs: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Check lots of cases
invariant.py only checks up to 100. sum_to is a recipe, so it can run for any n. Copy invariant.py once more:
cp invariant.py check.py
nvim check.py
Replace the last line, print(sum_to(100)), with a loop over many n (G, cc; after the assert line, Backspace once, so print comes after the loop, not inside it):
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        total = total + k
        assert 2 * total == k * (k + 1)
    return total

for n in range(1000):
    assert 2 * sum_to(n) == n * (n + 1)
print("all 1000 agree")
The recipe is unchanged. The new loop asks, for every n from 0 to 999, whether the loop and the formula agree (twice the sum against \(n(n+1)\), so no dividing). Run it:
python3 check.py
It prints all 1000 agree. Is the formula now true for every number? Decide before you read on.
No. A thousand examples is still just examples. Mathematicians have found patterns that held for millions of cases and then broke.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Why it can never fail
A claim that stays true after every round is a loop invariant, like the assert in invariant.py. Now the big question: if the assert passed in one round, why must it pass in the next? (What does one round add to total?) Decide before you read on.
Say it passed in the round for \(k - 1\):
\[2 \cdot \text{total} = (k-1)k\]
The next round, for \(k\), adds \(k\), so \(2 \cdot \text{total}\) grows by \(2k\):
\[(k-1)k + 2k = k(k+1)\]
which is exactly what the assert checks. It passes in the first round, and each passing round makes the next one pass, so it can never fail, however far the loop runs.
That’s no longer a check. It’s a proof for every \(n\), and it’s the method from maths class: induction. The first round is the first domino, and each round knocks over the next.
Write this proof on paper, in your own words. You’ll need it in the last session.






NoteTry it yourself




Add up the odd numbers 1 + 3 + 5 + … and print the running total for the first 10. What pattern do you see? Why would it hold? (Try drawing it with dots.)
Ask Claude: “Write a short Python function that adds up 1 to n, with one hidden bug. Don’t tell me where.” Find the bug by reasoning first, then prove it with a check.

section: Why AI and Lean belong together
text:
Why AI and Lean belong together
A proof that sounds right can still be wrong, and Claude is very good at sounding right. Lean doesn’t care how convincing a proof sounds: it checks every step, or it refuses. So the AI suggests, and Lean checks.
That leaves you the most important job: does the claim say what you meant? Lean checks that the proof proves the claim, not that it’s the claim you wanted.
crumbs: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
What Lean is
Lean is another programming language. It has boxes and loops, like Python, and it can also check proofs. Seeing the same program in a second language shows which parts are the ideas (a box, a repeat) and which are just spelling.
We’ll use Lean in the browser, with Claude beside it. Claude in Chrome is Claude in a side panel of Chrome that can read the page you’re on and type into it. Install the Claude extension from the Chrome Web Store, sign in, and pin it (the puzzle-piece icon, then the pin).
Open live.lean-lang.org, delete what’s there, and paste:
def sumLoop (n : Nat) : Nat := Id.run do
  let mut total := 0
  for k in [1:n+1] do
    total := total + k
  return total

#eval sumLoop 100
The panel on the right shows 5050. Here it is next to sum_to from gauss.py (without its print):



Python
Lean

total = 0
let mut total := 0


for k in range(1, n + 1):
for k in [1:n+1] do


total = total + k
total := total + k


return total

Nat is a natural number (0, 1, 2, …). (n : Nat) : Nat says n is one, and so is the answer.
let mut makes a box you can change (mutable).
:= puts something into a box, like Python’s =.
Id.run do says “steps, done in order”. Just copy it.
#eval runs a line and shows the answer.

To check your understanding: what does Lean make you say that Python doesn’t?

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Two programs, one answer
Gauss’s formula is a program too, a much faster one. Add it below:
def sumFormula (n : Nat) : Nat := n * (n + 1) / 2

#eval sumFormula 100
/ on natural numbers rounds down: 7 / 2 is 3. (Why doesn’t that rounding ever change the answer here?)
crumbs: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Checking isn’t proving
Do the two programs agree? Add one check, for \(n = 1000\):
#eval sumLoop 1000 == sumFormula 1000
It shows true. Now add the claim for every \(n\):
theorem agree (n : Nat) : sumLoop n = sumFormula n := by
  sorry
Read it out loud: “a claim called agree: for any natural number \(n\), the loop and the formula give the same answer. Proof: sorry.” This is check.py again, for every \(n\) instead of a thousand.
sorry means “I’ll prove this later”. Lean understands the claim but warns: declaration uses `sorry`. You still owe a proof, and checks like true don’t count. What Lean wants is an argument like your loop invariant.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
AI translates, Lean checks
Writing Lean proofs yourself comes later in the course. Today Claude only translates your proof, and you watch what Lean says.
Open Claude in Chrome on the Lean page, type in your paper proof from A thousand checks, then a proof, and ask:

Please prove agree in Lean by translating my proof, and see whether Lean accepts it. Don’t fix any mistakes in my proof, and don’t fix anything Lean complains about. Only translate my proof into Lean, and translate Lean’s answer back into English.

It may take a few minutes, and then Lean should accept it. Claude may add a smaller claim along the way (something like “one more round adds \(n + 1\)”). **Where is that step in your paper proof?
Next, a claim of my own. Before you send it, predict: is it true? Try \(n = 0\), 1 and 2 on paper. Then ask:

Now I want to check whether this also means that sum(n)^2 = n^3. Please convert that to Lean, have Lean check it, and translate only Lean’s answer back into English. Don’t fix the proof.

What did Lean say? And did Claude do only what you asked, or did it quietly change the claim to one that works?

title: Linear algebra 1: same arrow, new recipe
text:
The dictionary
You’ve been dragging b₁ and b₂ wherever you like. Now let’s fix one example and work it by hand. If you moved them, put them back where they started:

the old basis B is b₁ = (4, 1) and b₂ = (−6, 1);
the new basis C is the usual grid, c₁ one step right and c₂ one step up;
the arrow is x, whose coordinates in B are \([x]_B = (3, 1)\).

The question: what are x’s coordinates in C, \([x]_C\)?







How do we turn \([x]_B = (3, 1)\) into \([x]_C = (6, 4)\) without drawing?
Look up each basis vector of B in c-words, like words in a dictionary.


What is b₁, in c-words?
4c₁ + c₂, or the column (4, 1).


And b₂?
−6c₁ + c₂, or the column (−6, 1).


So what is 3b₁ + b₂?
3(4c₁ + c₂) + (−6c₁ + c₂) = 6c₁ + 4c₂. Coordinates (6, 4).


Where is the matrix?
Push the two columns together.



\[
P = \begin{pmatrix} {\color{#7570B3}4} & {\color{#D95F02}-6} \\ {\color{#7570B3}1} & {\color{#D95F02}1} \end{pmatrix}
\]
Column 1 is b₁; column 2 is b₂.







What is P(3, 1)?
3 of column 1, plus 1 of column 2: (6, 4).


Where have we seen that?
In the coloured line under the drag picture. Drag b₁, and column 1 changes with it.


So what is P?
A dictionary. Each column is one basis vector of B, looked up in C: \([b_1]_C\) and \([b_2]_C\).


What does Lay call it?
The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C, \(P_{C\leftarrow B}\), with \([x]_C = P_{C\leftarrow B}\,[x]_B\) (4.7).









NoteThe Law of Change of Coordinates



To change coordinates from B to C, write each vector of B in C’s coordinates. Those are the columns of \(P_{C\leftarrow B}\).









A friend writes \(P_{C\leftarrow B}\) with its columns as rows: \(\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ -6 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\). What do they get for (3, 1)?
(13, −17).


Is that x?
No. x is (6, 4).


What went wrong?
Each row mixes parts of b₁ and b₂. A column holds one whole basis vector.



To check your understanding, here is Lay’s 4.4, Example 1. The basis is b₁ = (1, 0) and b₂ = (1, 2), and \([x]_B = (-2, 3)\). What is x? Decide before you read on.







What is −2·b₁ + 3·b₂?
−2·(1, 0) + 3·(1, 2) = (1, 6).

title: Linear algebra 1: same arrow, new recipe
text:
Why anyone bothers
\[
A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
\]







Where does A send (1, 0)?
To (2, 1). Stretched and turned.


Where does A send (1, 1)?
To (3, 3).


Turned?
No. Same direction, three times as long.


And (−1, 1)?
To (−1, 1). It doesn’t move at all.











Along (1, 1) and (−1, 1), what does A do?
Only stretches: by 3, and by 1.


If those were our basis, what would A do to coordinates?
Multiply the first by 3 and leave the second alone: the matrix (3 0; 0 1). Same A, new matrix, as simple as a matrix gets.


How do we find such a basis?
That is part 2.

title: Linear algebra 3: coordinates that measure
text:
Cover the right-hand column. Answer each question in your head, then look.
Part 2 found A’s two eigenvectors:
\[
A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\qquad
v_1 = (1, 1),\ \text{eigenvalue } 3\qquad
v_2 = (-1, 1),\ \text{eigenvalue } 1
\]
It ended with a hint: they are perpendicular. This part is about why that matters. In a perpendicular basis, a coordinate stops being a bookkeeping number and becomes a measurement.

title: Linear algebra 3: coordinates that measure
section: A coordinate that depends on its neighbours
text:
A coordinate that depends on its neighbours








Both pictures have the same x = (6, 4) and the same b₁ = (4, 1). What changed?
Only b₂: (−6, 1) on the left, (0, 1) on the right.


How much b₁ is in x, on the left?
3, part 1’s coordinates: x = 3b₁ + b₂.


And on the right?
1.5: 1.5·(4, 1) + 2.5·(0, 1) = (6, 4).


b₁ didn’t move. Why did its coordinate change?
Coordinates are found together, by solving a·b₁ + b·b₂ = x. Move b₂, and a must change to make up for it.


So is “how much b₁ is in x” a question about x and b₁?
No. It’s a question about the whole basis.


Can a coordinate depend only on x and its own direction?
Yes, when the basis vectors are perpendicular.



Solving like this is how Lay finds coordinates in 4.4, Example 4: b₁ = (2, 1), b₂ = (−1, 1), x = (4, 5); 2a − b = 4 and a + b = 5 give \([x]_B = (3, 2)\). Those b’s aren’t perpendicular, so solving was the only way.

title: Linear algebra 3: coordinates that measure
Linear algebra 3: coordinates that measure
text:
Lengths come out right
A measurement should also get lengths right. Does a coordinate?







In part 1’s basis, x = (6, 4) has coordinates (3, 1). What is 3² + 1²?
10.


What is x’s length squared, 6² + 4²?
52. Those coordinates don’t know how long x is.


In our v’s, x = (2, 0) has coordinates (1, −1). What is 1² + (−1)²?
2. But x’s length squared is 4. Closer, still wrong.


Why?
Each v has length √2, not 1. A coordinate counts v’s, and each v is longer than a unit.



So make each basis vector length 1. Dividing each v by its length, which Lay writes ‖v‖ = √(v·v) (6.1), here √2, is called normalizing; the result is a unit vector. Call them u₁ and u₂. Orthogonal and of length 1, they are orthonormal.







What are x’s coordinates in u’s?
Measure: x·u₁ = 2/√2 = √2, and x·u₂ = −2/√2 = −√2. No dividing by u·u, which is 1.


What is (√2)² + (−√2)²?
2 + 2 = 4. x’s length squared, at last.


Is that luck?
No. It is Pythagoras: x is √2 of u₁ plus −√2 of u₂, at a right angle.


Do angles come out right too?
Yes. Dot products of coordinates equal dot products of the arrows, and angles come from dot products.









NoteThe Law of Length



In an orthonormal basis, ‖x‖² is the sum of the squares of x’s coordinates. Lengths and angles read off the coordinates are the true ones.

title: Linear algebra 3: coordinates that measure
section: An orthonormal basis is a turned grid
text:
An orthonormal basis is a turned grid
Put u₁ and u₂ in a matrix as columns. Lay keeps the name P, as in part 2; the difference is that its columns now have length 1:
\[
P = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} {\color{#7570B3}1} & {\color{#D95F02}-1} \\ {\color{#7570B3}1} & {\color{#D95F02}1} \end{pmatrix}\qquad
P^{\mathsf T} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} {\color{#7570B3}1} & {\color{#7570B3}1} \\ {\color{#D95F02}-1} & {\color{#D95F02}1} \end{pmatrix}
\]







What is Pᵀ?
P’s columns laid down as rows. Say “P transpose”.


What does Pᵀ do to x?
Each row is a u, so each entry is a measurement x·u: x’s coordinates in u’s.


So what undoes P?
Pᵀ. In part 2, P⁻¹ had to be worked out; here it is P read sideways.


Look back at part 2’s P⁻¹, (½ ½; −½ ½). What was it?
The v’s as rows, halved: the measurements, divided by v·v = 2.


What does P do to the page?
Turns it by 45°: it sends (1, 0) to u₁. Pᵀ turns it back.


What does a turn keep?
More than any other change of basis: eigenvalues and area, as every change of basis does (part 2), and lengths and angles too.


What does Lay call such a P?
An orthogonal matrix: square, orthonormal columns, P⁻¹ = Pᵀ. In 6.2 he names one U.



Part 2’s three steps become turn back, stretch, turn:
\[
A = P\,D\,P^{\mathsf T}\qquad
D = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\]








In the second picture, where are u₁ and u₂?
Along the usual grid. Pᵀ turned them there.


What does D do to the circle?
Stretches it three times wider, along u₁.


And the last step?
P turns everything back. x lands at (4, 2), as in part 2.









NoteThe Law of the Turn



An orthonormal basis is the usual grid, turned. A = P D Pᵀ: turn back, stretch, turn. A symmetric matrix is a pure stretch along perpendicular axes.

title: Linear algebra 3: coordinates that measure
text:
Why A’s eigenvectors are orthogonal
A is symmetric: flip it across its diagonal and it is unchanged. The 1 above the diagonal matches the 1 below it.
We’ll work out one number, (Av₁)·v₂, in two ways.







First way: A stretches v₁ by 3. So what is (Av₁)·v₂?
3(v₁·v₂).


Second way: move A across the dot, onto v₂. Is (Av₁)·v₂ the same as v₁·(Av₂)?
For symmetric A, yes. That’s the one fact we need; it’s checked below.


A stretches v₂ by 1. So what is v₁·(Av₂)?
1(v₁·v₂).


Both ways give the same number. So 3(v₁·v₂) = v₁·v₂. Which number is three times itself?
Only 0. So v₁·v₂ = 0: orthogonal.



Why can A move across the dot? Write out both sides for any v and w:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(Av)\cdot w &= (2v_1 + {\color{#D95F02}1}v_2)\,w_1 + ({\color{#D95F02}1}v_1 + 2v_2)\,w_2\\
v\cdot(Aw) &= v_1\,(2w_1 + {\color{#D95F02}1}w_2) + v_2\,({\color{#D95F02}1}w_1 + 2w_2)
\end{aligned}
\]







Multiply out. Which terms does each line have?
Both have 2v₁w₁, 2v₂w₂, v₂w₁ and v₁w₂. Equal.


Which number did that rely on?
The two orange 1s being the same: A’s symmetry.


What if A were part 4’s matrix (3 0; 4 5)?
Its corners differ (0 and 4), the two sides differ, and its eigenvectors aren’t orthogonal.









NoteThe Law of Symmetry



A symmetric matrix can move across a dot product. So its eigenvectors, with different eigenvalues, are orthogonal.


To check your understanding, here is Lay’s 7.1, Example 4:
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 7 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}
\]







Is it symmetric?
Yes: the 2 above the diagonal matches the 2 below it.


Where does it send (2, 1)? And (−1, 2)?
To (16, 8) = 8·(2, 1), and to (−3, 6) = 3·(−1, 2). Eigenvectors, with eigenvalues 8 and 3.


Are they orthogonal?
(2, 1)·(−1, 2) = −2 + 2 = 0. Yes, as the Law says.

title: Linear algebra 3: coordinates that measure
text:
Keep only the biggest part
A measurement lets us do one more thing: throw coordinates away. Back to part 1’s x = (6, 4), and keep only what lies along b₁ = (4, 1).








In part 1’s basis, x’s b₁ part is 3b₁. Where is it?
(12, 3), about 6.1 from x. Far off.


Now take x’s projection onto b₁’s line instead. Where is it?
(28/17)·(4, 1), about (6.6, 1.6): about 2.4 from x.


Is any point on that line closer to x?
No. The dashed line meets it at a right angle, so the projection is the nearest point.


Which basis keeps exactly that point?
An orthonormal one with u₁ along b₁. Its first coordinate is a measurement, so keeping it alone is as close as that direction can get.









NoteThe Law of the Nearest Point



In an orthonormal basis, keep only some coordinates, and you get the nearest point those directions can reach: the projection.









Do these three laws need A to be symmetric?
No. Measuring, lengths and nearest points hold in any orthonormal basis. Symmetry only makes A’s eigenvectors one.


Most matrices aren’t symmetric. Is that the end?
No. Part 4 gives every matrix an orthonormal basis going in and another coming out, then uses the nearest point to find the best line through data.

title: Lesson 1.5 (draft): How long will the money last?
text:
Guess first
Let’s say we had $500,000 and we want to spend $20,000 a year. Well, then we know that in 25 years we’ll run out of money. It’ll all be gone.
We’ve also heard of interest. If we put the $500,000 in a bank, we’ll get some more money every year. So what if we were to make 2% interest every year? Will the money last longer than 25 years, if we spend $20,000 a year?
Now, another thing that happens over the years, especially over, say, 25 years, is that things get more expensive. 25 years ago, a meal probably cost a lot less. You could probably get french fries and a hamburger for $5, and today that might cost $10. If you are buying hamburgers, you may have to spend more each year. That’s called inflation.
But you might be getting money from interest, and the money you get from interest might be a little more than the money you have to spend from inflation. Suppose your money earns 5% interest and there’s 4% inflation. Then in a real sense you’re getting 1% more value per year. So how does that affect how long the money will last?
Remember, in this second part you’re not spending $20,000 a year. You’re spending $20,000 worth every year, based on the first year’s prices.
Write your guesses down before reading on. Nobody will check them. That’s the point.

Where to now? Both roads end up in the same place.

Did people 800 years ago worry about this too?
I just want to see if my guess was right.

section: Meet the man who asked first
text:
Meet the man who asked first



Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci. The picture is from 1850, so it’s a bit of a guess what he might have looked like. (Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.)


Most people know Fibonacci for coming up with a sequence where you take the two previous numbers and add them. You might start with 1, 1. Add them, you get 2. Then you add the two previous ones: 1 plus 2 is 3, 2 plus 3 is 5. So the Fibonacci sequence is 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, …
It has a lot of interesting history and all kinds of deep connections. It connects out to something called the golden ratio, which is what makes certain things look very aesthetic. They say the Parthenon follows the golden ratio in terms of its height versus its width. I’m not sure why, but that’s what I’ve found out.
But what’s interesting here is his Liber Abaci (“The Book of Calculation”). He wrote it in 1202, so this is a long time ago. It was where he showed merchants, Italian merchants, how to use Hindu–Arabic numerals to find profits, convert money from one country’s currency to another’s, and work out interest. And interest is what we’re looking at here.
Somewhere in there is a problem that’s basically ours: someone has money in the bank and takes a fixed amount out each year. When does it run out?

title: Lesson 1.5 (draft): How long will the money last?
text:
The pattern
At $5,000 a year the balance never moves, because you’re spending exactly the interest (1% of $500,000 = $5,000). Spend less than the interest and the pile grows forever. Spend more and it shrinks, and it shrinks faster each year, because a smaller pile earns less interest. That’s why the last few years of the spreadsheet drop so steeply.






NotePercentages · Try it



Your spreadsheet has a “Continuous formula” cell up top that says the money lasts about 28.8 years. Your table ran out in year 29. Two completely different methods agree. Whenever two methods agree, you can trust both a bit more. You’ll use this trick all through the book.



The crossroads. You have the whole idea now, and stopping here is a complete chapter. If one of these questions is nagging at you, follow it. Every box ends with a way back here.

Could I get the answer on a calculator in one step? logarithms · a little Python
How can adding numbers up forever give an ordinary number? geometric series
What if the stock market crashes the year I start spending? simulation · Python
What if the money grew every second, not once a year? differential equations
Couldn’t I just ask a chatbot? no new math



Or a question about the machine:

How does a chatbot choose its next word? exponentials · a little Python
Can anyone see what’s going on inside when it adds? interpretability








NoteLogarithms · a formula instead of a table





The table works, but it takes 29 rows. The shortcut needs two functions from precalculus.
The exponential is one of the most important functions in business because it represents continuously compounded return
\[
FV = PV e^{rt}
\]
We begin with logarithms, which are the inverse of the exponential. In this course, just like we use \(e\) as the default base for an exponential function, we use the natural log \(\ln\) as the default logarithm.
With those two, the table collapses into one line:
\[
T = \frac{1}{r}\,\ln\!\frac{c}{c - rW}
\]
where \(W\) is the nest egg, \(c\) is yearly spending and \(r\) is the interest rate (as a decimal). With our numbers, \(T = 100 \ln(20000/15000) \approx 28.8\) years.
Notice what happens when \(c = rW\) (spending equals interest): the bottom of the fraction is zero, and the formula says “forever”. That’s the pattern you found in the spreadsheet.
Here’s the same thing in Python, checked against the year-by-year method:

from math import log

W0, c, r = 500_000, 20_000, 0.01

# year by year, like the spreadsheet
W, years = W0, 0
while W > 0:
    W = W * (1 + r) - c
    years += 1

T = log(c / (c - r * W0)) / r      # the shortcut formula
print(f"year by year: runs out during year {years}")
print(f"formula:      T = {T:.1f} years")

year by year: runs out during year 29
formula:      T = 28.8 years



Next: How can adding up forever give an ordinary number? · What if the money grew every second? · ↩︎ Back to the crossroads










NoteSoftmax · how a chatbot turns scores into odds





A chatbot writes one token at a time. At each step it gives every token in its dictionary a score: bigger means “more likely to come next”. Scores can be any number, even negative, so they aren’t probabilities yet.
To turn scores into probabilities it uses the same \(e\) as continuous compounding. Raise \(e\) to each score, then divide by the total:
\[
p_i = \frac{e^{s_i}}{\sum_j e^{s_j}}
\]
This is called softmax. The exponential makes every number positive, and dividing by the total makes them add up to 1. And just as compounding turns a small difference in interest rate into a big difference in money, the exponential turns a small lead in score into a big lead in probability: a score 1 higher means \(e \approx 2.7\) times as likely.
Here the model has just written “The money will last 28.” and is choosing the next token:

from math import exp

scores = {"8": 3.0, "9": 2.0, "7": 1.0, "5": -1.0}   # made-up scores

total = sum(exp(s) for s in scores.values())
probs = {tok: exp(s) / total for tok, s in scores.items()}
for tok, p in probs.items():
    print(f"'{tok}': {p:.3f}")

# second check: probabilities add to 1, and a score 1 higher is e times as likely
print(f"sum = {sum(probs.values()):.6f}")
print(f"p('8') / p('9') = {probs['8'] / probs['9']:.4f}  vs  e = {exp(1):.4f}")

'8': 0.657
'9': 0.242
'7': 0.089
'5': 0.012
sum = 1.000000
p('8') / p('9') = 2.7183  vs  e = 2.7183


So the model will most likely write “28.8”, but about one time in four it writes “28.9”, which is where the confident-but-wrong answers come from. Some chatbots let you set a temperature: dividing every score by a number bigger than 1 flattens the differences, so the model takes more chances.

↩︎ Back to the crossroads · Couldn’t I just ask a chatbot?










NoteSeries · why the table has a formula at all





Each year the money you still have grows by a factor of \(1.01\), and another $20,000 comes out. Add up all those withdrawals and their lost interest and you get a geometric series.
A series is the sum of a sequence — an infinite sum. The sum of an infinite list of numbers can either be finite, so the series can converge to a number, or the sum can be infinite, so the series diverges.
We start with the basic geometric series:
\[S = 1+r+r^2+r^3+r^4+\cdots\]
Here \(r\) is a constant, the series converges when \(|r|<1\) and diverges when \(1\leq|r|\). In fact, we can find what number the infinite geometric series converges to. Write the series out for \(Sr\):
\[Sr = r+r^2+r^3+r^4+r^5+\cdots\]
Looks a lot like the series for \(S\) itself. Now subtract:
\[S-Sr=1\]
All the terms cancel! And then solve for \(S\):
\[S=\frac1{1-r}=1+r+r^2+r^3+r^4+\cdots\]
Now that we know \(S\), we can easily find other finite sums like
\[1+r+r^2+\cdots+r^{321}=S-Sr^{322}=S(1-r^{322})=\frac{1-r^{322}}{1-r}\]
For the money, the ratio is \(1.01\) instead of \(r\), and we stop after \(n\) years instead of going on forever. Set the balance to zero and solve for \(n\):
\[
n = \frac{\ln\big(c/(c - rW)\big)}{\ln(1+r)} = \frac{\ln(4/3)}{\ln 1.01} \approx 28.9 \text{ years,}
\]
which matches the spreadsheet (year 29) even better than the continuous 28.8.

Next: What if the money grew every second? · ↩︎ Back to the crossroads










NoteSimulation · what if returns are random?





Real investments don’t pay a steady 1%. Some years are great, some are terrible. Let’s say returns average 3% but swing a lot, then simulate 10,000 possible futures and count how many run out within 30 years:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n, years = 10_000, 30
returns = rng.normal(0.03, 0.12, size=(n, years))

W = np.full(n, 500_000.0)
paths = np.empty((n, years))
for t in range(years):
    W = np.maximum(W * (1 + returns[:, t]) - 20_000, 0)
    paths[:, t] = W

print(f"ran out within {years} years: {(paths[:, -1] == 0).mean():.1%}")

plt.plot(paths[:50].T / 1000, lw=0.7, alpha=0.6)
plt.xlabel("year"); plt.ylabel("balance ($ thousands)")
plt.title("50 of the 10,000 simulated futures");

ran out within 30 years: 36.5%









The average return (3%) is higher than before, yet about a third of the futures still run dry. Bad years early on hurt the most, because they shrink the pile right when it has the most growing left to do.

Next: What if the money grew every second? · ↩︎ Back to the crossroads · Couldn’t I just ask a chatbot?










NoteDifferential equations · where the formula comes from





Treat time as continuous. The balance changes at the rate interest in minus spending out:
\[
\frac{dW}{dt} = rW - c, \qquad W(0) = W_0 .
\]
That’s a differential equation.
If \(f(x)\) is a function, then \(f'(x)\) or \(df/dx\) is its derivative. We can make equations involving them. In these equations, we solve for \(f(x)\) using integration. We can also plug in functions by taking their derivatives to see whether they satisfy a differential equation.
For instance, we can look at the equation \(f' = k f\), and then we can try \(f=\cos(x)\). Then \(f'(x)=-\sin(x)\), so when we plug in we get \(\cos(x)=-k\sin(x)\). These are unequal so \(f=\cos(x)\) does not solve the equation. Next we can try \(f=e^{kx}\) so that \(f'=k e^{kx}\). Plugging in we get \(ke^{kx}=k e^{kx}\) so that \(f=e^{kx}\) does solve the equation.
Our money equation is almost \(f' = kf\), just with the \(-c\) tacked on. So try an exponential plus a constant, and plug in. It works:
\[
W(t) = \frac{c}{r} + \left(W_0 - \frac{c}{r}\right)e^{rt}.
\]
Set \(W(T) = 0\) and solve for \(T\) to get the logarithm formula. The quantity \(c/r\) is the balance whose interest exactly pays for the spending: start above it and you grow forever, start below it and you hit zero.
Your spreadsheet was solving this equation all along.



Leonhard Euler in 1753, pastel by Jakob Emanuel Handmann. He had already lost the sight of his right eye in the late 1730s, and went on to publish more mathematics than almost anyone in history. (Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.)


A differential equation \(y'(x)=f(x,y)\) specifies the slope of a solution curve \(y(x)\) at any point \((x,y)\) in the plane. Suppose we want to estimate the solution \(y(x)\) with a given initial value \(y(x_0)=y_0\). This can be done more simply by realizing that the slope is the “rise-over-run”, so the \(\Delta y = f(x,y)\Delta x\) is how much the \(y\) increases when we take a step \(\Delta x\).
For us \(f = rW - c\) and the step is one year, so \(\Delta W = rW - c\): interest minus spending, which is exactly one row of the spreadsheet. The 29-row table is Euler’s method with \(\Delta t = 1\). That’s why it lands close to, but not exactly on, the continuous answer of 28.8 years.
The random version, where returns are noisy and your lifetime is uncertain too, is Milevsky’s seventh equation, named for Andrey Kolmogorov. It gives the probability of outliving your money.

↩︎ Back to the crossroads · Couldn’t I just ask a chatbot?










NoteInterpretability · watching a model add





Can we look inside a model and see how it does a sum? A new field called interpretability tries to do exactly that. Researchers trace which parts of the model light up, and what each part contributes, as it works.
In 2025, researchers at Anthropic traced one of their models adding \(36 + 59\). It didn’t carry the one. It ran two paths side by side:

one path made a rough estimate of the size, something like “a bit over 90”;
another worked out only the last digit exactly: 6 + 9 ends in 5.

Put together, “a bit over 90” and “ends in 5” give 95. That’s a strange way to add, but it works, and nobody taught it that. It found the method on its own while learning to predict text.
Here’s the part worth remembering. When they then asked the model how it got 95, it described the school method: add the ones, carry the one, add the tens. Its explanation was a sensible story, but it wasn’t what it had actually done.
So checking a chatbot means checking two things: its answer (against your spreadsheet) and its explanation (which may be a plausible story rather than a report).

↩︎ Back to the crossroads · Couldn’t I just ask a chatbot?

title: Lesson 1.5 (draft): How long will the money last?
text:
Using AI
Ask an AI assistant: “I have $500,000, spend $20,000 a year and earn 1%. How many years will it last?”
Then check its answer against your spreadsheet. AI chatbots are often shaky at arithmetic, even when they sound very sure of themselves. If it’s wrong, can you work out what it did? Now ask it to write a spreadsheet formula or Python code for the problem instead of answering directly, and check that. Which way worked better?

What the chatbot sees
When you type “I have $500,000”, the chatbot never sees the number the way you do. Before anything else happens, your text is chopped into tokens: short chunks that the model has a numbered list of, a bit like a dictionary where every entry has a page number. The model only ever sees the page numbers.
Long numbers usually get chopped too. Many chatbots cut digits into chunks of up to three, so 500,000 might arrive as 500 · , · 000: three tokens, and nothing in them says “this 500 means five hundred thousand”. You learned place value in second grade. The model has to work it out from patterns in everything it read.
That’s one reason a chatbot can explain compound interest beautifully and still get the arithmetic wrong. Explaining is about patterns in words, which is what it’s built for. Arithmetic is about place value, which it never sees directly.

title: Trigonometry 2: the wave
text:
The tides

A harbour: high tide is 9 m deep at 3 am, low tide 1 m at 9 am, high again at 3 pm.







The midline?
Halfway between 9 and 1: 5 m.


The amplitude?
From the midline to the top: 9 − 5 = 4 m.


The period?
High tide to high tide: 12 hours.


So B?
Period = 2π/B, so B = 2π/12 = π/6.


sin or cos?
cos starts at its top. High tide is at 3, so slide cos right by 3.


The model?
depth = 5 + 4 cos(π/6 · (t − 3)), t in hours after midnight.


How deep at 7 am?
5 + 4 cos(π/6 · 4) = 5 + 4 cos(2π/3).



Decide before you read on.
2π/3 is 120°, and cos 120° = −1/2 (part 1). So the depth is 5 + 4 · (−1/2) = 3 m.

y = 2 sin(3x) − 1. Give the amplitude, period, midline, highest and lowest values.


Answer

Amplitude 2, period 2π/3, midline y = −1; highest −1 + 2 = 1, lowest −1 − 2 = −3.

Sketch y = cos x + 2 from 0 to 2π. Mark its midline, its top and its bottom.


Answer

Midline y = 2. Top 3 at x = 0 and 2π; bottom 1 at x = π.

Where does csc x break between 0 and 2π? Where is tan x zero?


Answer

csc breaks where sin x = 0: 0, π, 2π. tan x = sin x ÷ cos x is zero where sin x is: also 0, π, 2π.

In the harbour, how deep is it at 9 am? At which four times of day is it exactly 5 m deep?


Answer

1 m (low tide). 5 m is the midline, crossed halfway between high and low: midnight, 6 am, noon and 6 pm.

Luckily you can delay gratification: for example, you profit by learning basic vim editing commands, so you actually have the most powerful tool at your fingertips. Don’t take the cookie, invest about 5 more minutes - yes it looks complicated at first, but hold on, it’s actually simple and fast, and you’ll get 2 more cookies.
The bash commands you need:
git config merge.tool vimdiff git config merge.conflictstyle diff3 git config mergetool.prompt false git mergetool
